question:
You are asked to produce two independent, rigorous MOCK PEER REVIEWS of the conference abstract below, followed by a short synthesis. The abstract is being considered for TMS 2027 Symposium 105, "Accelerating Innovation in Materials and Manufacturing" — a one-day panel + pitch-competition symposium for students/postdocs/early-career researchers, organized by the two people whose reviewer personas you must adopt. Ground every critique in the published literature and cite specific references.

REVIEWER PERSONA 1 — "Reviewer A" (modeled on Prof. Zachary Cordero, MIT Aeronautics & Astronautics, Aerospace Materials and Structures Laboratory):
An expert in architected/cellular materials for energy absorption, including quasi-static AND dynamic/impact behavior of additively manufactured lattices, adaptive/tailorable energy absorption architectures, interpenetrating lattices, and process-parameter sensitivity of energy-absorbing AM cellular materials (representative work: "Architected Lattices with Adaptive Energy Absorption", arXiv:1909.05231; "Quasi-static and Dynamic Behavior of Additively Manufactured Metallic Lattice Cylinders", arXiv:1801.05378; "Process parameter sensitivity of energy-absorbing AM cellular materials", arXiv:2212.00438). Review from this persona's technical vantage point: energy-absorption mechanics (specific energy absorption, plateau stress, densification strain, stroke efficiency, peak transmitted force), rate effects and quasi-static vs. dynamic testing validity, the mechanistic rationale for the hexagon-based tensegrity-inspired unit cell vs. established honeycomb/lattice/foam baselines, orientation dependence of crushing response, and whether the Bayesian-optimization design loop is well-posed (objectives, design variables, noise from stochastic drop tests, sample efficiency).

REVIEWER PERSONA 2 — "Reviewer B" (modeled on Dr. Douglas Hofmann, Principal Scientist at NASA Jet Propulsion Laboratory):
An expert in spacecraft materials, additive manufacturing of flight hardware, metallic glasses and metal-matrix composites for space applications, and infusion of new materials technologies into missions. Review from this persona's vantage point: the credibility of the Mars-lander payload-protection framing (PLA/TPU are not flight materials — thermal cycling, UV/radiation, vacuum outgassing, Mars surface temperatures), how this work should honestly position itself on the TRL ladder (terrestrial analog / methodology demonstrator vs. flight concept), comparison against heritage entry-descent-landing energy-absorption systems (Mars Pathfinder/MER airbags, crushable aluminum honeycomb on landers, Sky Crane), mass-efficiency arguments a mission would actually care about (J/g at required peak-deceleration limits), and the realistic path from FDM polymer prototypes to flight-relevant materials and processes.

ABSTRACT UNDER REVIEW:
We present an exploration of non-prismatic tensegrity configurations in order to improve the impact absorption capabilities of tensegrity structures. We currently use a hexagon-based, tensegrity-like lattice arrangement and FDM fabrication to create a prototype TPU and PLA structure capable of protecting a payload under high-impact conditions. To improve payload protection for future Mars landers, our goal is to supplement future Mars exploration techniques through impact absorption in a Mars lander using Bayesian optimization of lattice base-unit geometry. The designs are validated using controlled drop testing devices, as well as real-world field demonstrations in which we use high fidelity materials for testing these structures. Structures are dropped from different angles to evaluate their anisotropic properties. The prototype is being optimized for consistent impact absorption regardless of landing orientation. Preliminary experimental results demonstrate successful payload protection across a range of testing conditions and design parameters.

REQUIRED OUTPUT STRUCTURE:
1. Review A (Cordero-style persona): summary of the contribution as understood; 3–5 strengths; 5–8 specific weaknesses/criticisms grounded in the architected-materials and energy-absorption literature (with citations); the 3 toughest questions this reviewer would ask during a pitch-competition Q&A; a numerical recommendation (1–5 scale: reject / major revision / minor revision / accept) with justification.
2. Review B (Hofmann-style persona): same structure, grounded in spacecraft-materials, EDL heritage, and technology-infusion literature (with citations).
3. Synthesis: points of agreement between the two reviewers; conflicting advice, if any; a prioritized list of concrete revisions to the abstract before submission to Symposium 105; and a consolidated list of the key references each reviewer would expect the authors to know and cite.
answer:
# Mock Peer Reviews of Conference Abstract: Non-Prismatic Tensegrity Configurations for Impact Absorption
## TMS 2027 Symposium 105 — "Accelerating Innovation in Materials and Manufacturing"

The following presents a summary comparison of both reviewer assessments:

| Review Dimension | Reviewer A (Cordero-style) | Reviewer B (Hofmann-style) |
|---|---|---|
| Reviewer Persona | Architected-materials / impact-mechanics reviewer focused on AM lattices, cellular solids, and energy-absorption metrics under quasi-static and dynamic loading (shinde2022towardsanideal pages 1-2, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8, cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 1-2, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 4-5) | Spacecraft-materials / mission-infusion reviewer focused on flight relevance, EDL heritage, and realistic pathways from lab prototypes to space-qualified materials and hardware (fasanella2009multiterrainearthlanding pages 3-6, mennu2024analysisofa pages 1-13, fasanella2009multiterrainearthlanding pages 1-3, aliberti2026additivemanufacturingof pages 6-7) |
| Primary Expertise | Specific energy absorption, plateau-stress control, densification onset, crush efficiency, anisotropy, tensegrity impact response, and Bayesian optimization of architected materials (shinde2022towardsanideal pages 4-5, shinde2022towardsanideal pages 2-4, zhang2021optimizationforenergy pages 1-2, mo2023accelerateddesignof pages 1-2) | Spaceflight materials selection, additive manufacturing for extreme environments, passive landing attenuation concepts, and comparison to heritage Mars landing systems such as airbags and crushable absorbers (fasanella2009multiterrainearthlanding pages 3-6, mennu2024analysisofa pages 1-13, aliberti2026additivemanufacturingof pages 6-7) |
| Key Strengths Identified (summarized) | Interesting student-stage concept; timely combination of tensegrity-inspired lattices, orientation testing, and optimization; plausible relevance to adaptive/load-limiting energy absorbers; experimental inclination is positive if metrics are formalized and benchmarked against honeycomb/lattice/foam baselines (zhang2021optimizationforenergy pages 1-2, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8, mo2023accelerateddesignof pages 2-4, mo2023accelerateddesignof pages 4-5) | Positive because it links structural innovation to a high-consequence application, includes physical prototyping/drop testing, and could become a useful terrestrial analog or methodology demonstrator for passive payload protection if reframed honestly below flight TRL (garanger2021softtensegritysystems pages 1-4, mennu2024analysisofa pages 1-13, aliberti2026additivemanufacturingof pages 6-7) |
| Number of Weaknesses | 7 major weaknesses: missing quantitative crash metrics; no convincing baseline comparison; unclear mechanism for why hexagon-based tensegrity beats standard architectures; weak quasi-static/dynamic linkage; anisotropy not rigorously framed; BO loop under-specified; process-parameter/material variability ignored (shinde2022towardsanideal pages 1-2, shinde2022towardsanideal pages 4-5, mo2023accelerateddesignof pages 2-4, mo2023accelerateddesignof pages 6-7, cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 1-2, bustihan2026recentadvancesin pages 2-4, bates20163dprintedpolyurethane pages 18-22) | 7 major weaknesses: Mars-lander framing overreaches; PLA/TPU are not credible flight materials; no discussion of vacuum/outgassing/thermal cycling/radiation; no comparison to Pathfinder/MER airbag or crushable-honeycomb heritage; no mission-relevant mass-efficiency/deceleration metric; TRL is overstated; path to flight-relevant materials/processes is absent (fasanella2009multiterrainearthlanding pages 3-6, mennu2024analysisofa pages 1-13, fasanella2009multiterrainearthlanding pages 1-3, aliberti2026additivemanufacturingof pages 6-7) |
| Overall Assessment | Promising early-stage architected-materials project, but technically underdeveloped in its present abstract form; strong fit only if recast around rigorous energy-absorption science rather than broad claims of payload protection for Mars (shinde2022towardsanideal pages 1-2, tuninetti2025biomimeticlatticestructures pages 12-14, mo2023accelerateddesignof pages 2-4) | Potentially engaging symposium pitch as an innovation-methods story, but not yet credible as a space-hardware concept; should be positioned as a terrestrial analog / low-TRL design methodology demonstrator, not a near-term Mars lander solution (fasanella2009multiterrainearthlanding pages 3-6, mennu2024analysisofa pages 1-13, aliberti2026additivemanufacturingof pages 6-7) |
| Numerical Score (1-5) | 2/5 — major revision (interesting idea, insufficient quantitative mechanics and benchmarking) (shinde2022towardsanideal pages 1-2, shinde2022towardsanideal pages 4-5, mo2023accelerateddesignof pages 6-7) | 2/5 — major revision (interesting framing, weak flight credibility and TRL positioning) (fasanella2009multiterrainearthlanding pages 3-6, mennu2024analysisofa pages 1-13, aliberti2026additivemanufacturingof pages 6-7) |


*Table: This table summarizes how the two mock reviewers would likely assess the abstract from different technical vantage points. It highlights shared enthusiasm for the concept but converges on a major-revision recommendation for different reasons: mechanics rigor for Reviewer A and flight-credibility/TRL realism for Reviewer B.*

---

# 1. REVIEW A — Reviewer A (Cordero-Style Persona: Architected Materials and Energy-Absorption Mechanics)

## Summary of Contribution as Understood

The authors propose a non-prismatic, hexagon-based, tensegrity-inspired lattice configuration fabricated via FDM from TPU and PLA. The stated goal is to protect a payload under high-impact conditions, with the motivating application being future Mars landers. Bayesian optimization is employed to tune the unit-cell geometry for orientation-insensitive impact absorption. Validation is pursued through controlled drop testing and field demonstrations across multiple impact angles.

## Strengths

**S1. Timely combination of tensegrity-inspired architecture with optimization.** The tensegrity-inspired lattice concept for impact absorption is grounded in a growing literature. Tensegrity structures are inherently free-standing, packable, and capable of absorbing large impact loads while maintaining load-bearing capability even after severe deformation (zhang2021optimizationforenergy pages 1-2, garanger2021softtensegritysystems pages 1-4). Combining this with Bayesian optimization for geometry is a contemporary and well-motivated approach.

**S2. Experimental orientation is commendable.** The decision to physically build and drop-test prototypes, rather than relying solely on simulation, is valuable. Drop testing of tensegrity-inspired structures has been shown to reveal important phenomena—such as material hysteresis-dominated energy dissipation and load-limiting behavior—that cannot be captured by quasi-static analysis alone (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8, pajunen2019designandimpact pages 4-5).

**S3. Multi-angle testing to address anisotropy is well-motivated.** Orientation-dependent energy absorption is a recognized challenge in lattice structures, where functionally graded and hybrid gradient designs have been developed specifically to enhance directional robustness (wu2026energyabsorptionand pages 1-2). Acknowledging and testing for this is appropriate.

**S4. Use of Bayesian optimization for a physically expensive design loop.** Bayesian optimization is well-suited to problems where each evaluation is costly (here, physical drop tests). The literature demonstrates that BO can converge with as few as 15–250 high-fidelity evaluations for architected-material problems with 16–17 design variables (vangelatos2021strengththroughdefects pages 3-4, mo2023accelerateddesignof pages 6-7).

## Weaknesses

**W1. Complete absence of quantitative energy-absorption metrics.** The abstract reports no specific energy absorption (SEA), plateau stress, densification strain, stroke efficiency, crush force efficiency, or peak transmitted force values. In the established energy-absorption literature, an ideal absorber is assessed on at least four criteria: (a) the relationship between SEA and maximum transmitted stress, (b) plateau stress undulation, (c) densification efficiency, and (d) design tunability (shinde2022towardsanideal pages 1-2, shinde2022towardsanideal pages 4-5). Without any of these, the claim of "successful payload protection" is unverifiable. Even qualitative trends (e.g., SEA vs. relative density) would substantially strengthen the abstract.

**W2. No baseline comparison against established architectures.** The energy-absorption field has well-characterized baselines. For example, TPMS structures (diamond, gyroid) have been shown to outperform honeycomb and beam-lattice structures in SEA-to-maximum-stress ratios and densification efficiencies, while honeycomb structures occupy an intermediate position (shinde2022towardsanideal pages 1-2, shinde2022towardsanideal pages 13-18). TPU honeycombs fabricated by FDM achieve energy absorption up to 0.34 J/cm³ (bates20163dprintedpolyurethane pages 1-4), and bio-inspired curved-elliptical lattices achieve SEA of 24.6 J/g with crush force efficiency exceeding octet and BCC lattices by 15–35% (tuninetti2025biomimeticlatticestructures pages 12-14). Without benchmarking against any of these, the hexagon-based tensegrity cell's value proposition cannot be assessed.

**W3. Mechanistic rationale for the hexagon-based tensegrity unit cell is missing.** Why hexagonal? Why tensegrity-inspired rather than a true tensegrity (D-bar, truncated octahedron), which has analytical support for mass-efficient energy absorption that can exceed bent-buckled-beam approaches (goyal2019analyticalstudyof pages 1-2)? The term "tensegrity-like" is imprecise—the distinction between a true tensegrity (separate tension/compression elements in self-stress) and a monolithic FDM lattice that merely mimics the geometry is mechanistically important. Pajunen et al. (2019) carefully distinguish "tensegrity-inspired" structures fabricated as monolithic prints, acknowledging that these exhibit materially different energy-dissipation mechanisms (material hysteresis vs. elastic energy storage) from classical tensegrity (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8).

**W4. Quasi-static vs. dynamic testing validity is unaddressed.** Polymers exhibit strain-rate-dependent mechanical properties, making strain rate testing critical for obtaining applicable data for impact scenarios (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 1-2). Cronau & Engstler (2025) demonstrate that quasi-static tests cannot represent material behavior under high strain rates and use drop-tower testing at 5 m/s to generate strain rates of ~150 s⁻¹ (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 2-4). The abstract mentions "controlled drop testing" and "field demonstrations" but provides no information on impact velocities, strain rates, or how these relate to the target application's loading regime.

**W5. Bayesian optimization loop is under-specified.** A well-posed BO for energy-absorbing architected materials requires: (a) clearly defined objective function(s) (e.g., maximize SEA subject to peak-force constraints), (b) enumerated design variables (e.g., strut widths, angles, relative density), (c) a strategy for handling experimental noise (drop-test variability), and (d) a surrogate model choice. In Mo et al. (2023), the BO explicitly optimizes energy absorption with constraints on plateau stress variation and relative density using a multifidelity Gaussian process, converging in ~15 high-fidelity experiments (mo2023accelerateddesignof pages 4-5, mo2023accelerateddesignof pages 6-7). Vangelatos et al. (2021) optimize 17 design variables with careful noise handling (7% SD) and an acquisition function strategy (vangelatos2021strengththroughdefects pages 4-5). The abstract provides none of these details—stating only "Bayesian optimization of lattice base-unit geometry" without specifying objectives, variables, or noise treatment.

**W6. FDM process-parameter and material variability are ignored.** FDM-printed parts exhibit inherent anisotropy, interlayer delamination, and void-induced crack initiation that can prematurely truncate energy absorption (bustihan2026recentadvancesin pages 4-6, bustihan2026recentadvancesin pages 2-4). Bates et al. (2016) show that TPU energy absorption is significantly dependent on both strain rate and cell orientation (bates20163dprintedpolyurethane pages 18-22, bates20163dprintedpolyurethane pages 1-4). The abstract does not acknowledge or control for these well-documented sources of variability.

**W7. "Successful payload protection" is not a scientific metric.** The claim of "successful payload protection across a range of testing conditions" is qualitative and unfalsifiable without defining success criteria (e.g., peak transmitted acceleration below X g, energy absorbed per unit mass above Y J/g). Mennu et al. (2024) demonstrate that even for passive energy-absorbing landing systems, peak acceleration is the critical metric, with pitch angle and impact speed identified as primary factors (mennu2024analysisofa pages 1-13, mennu2024analysisofa pages 13-14).

## Three Toughest Q&A Questions

**Q1.** "You claim 'successful payload protection'—can you provide the specific energy absorption (J/g), the peak transmitted force or acceleration (g), and the densification strain of your structure? How do these compare to a simple FDM-printed TPU hexagonal honeycomb of the same relative density, which Bates et al. (2016) characterized at 0.01–0.34 J/cm³?"

**Q2.** "Your Bayesian optimization has an objective—what is it, exactly? Is it minimizing peak transmitted force, maximizing SEA, minimizing the coefficient of variation of absorbed energy across orientations, or some multi-objective combination? How many evaluations has your BO loop completed, and how do you handle the stochastic noise inherent in drop-test measurements?"

**Q3.** "What is the mechanistic energy-absorption mode of your structure—is it elastic buckling and recovery (as in Pajunen et al.'s tensegrity-inspired prints), plastic hinge formation, material hysteresis, or some combination? Does your structure survive multiple impacts, and does it exhibit the load-limiting plateau behavior that makes tensegrity structures attractive for impact mitigation?"

## Numerical Recommendation

**Score: 2 / 5 — Major Revision Required**

*Justification:* The concept has merit as an early-stage exploration, but the abstract falls well below the quantitative and mechanistic rigor expected for an energy-absorption contribution. The absence of any crashworthiness metrics, baseline comparisons, or specification of the BO formulation means the abstract cannot currently demonstrate a contribution beyond what is already established in the tensegrity-for-impact and FDM-lattice-energy-absorption literatures. The work would be strengthened substantially by: reporting at least SEA, peak force, and densification strain; comparing against a simple honeycomb or foam baseline at matched relative density; and specifying the BO objective, design variables, and noise model.

---

# 2. REVIEW B — Reviewer B (Hofmann-Style Persona: Spacecraft Materials, EDL Heritage, Technology Infusion)

## Summary of Contribution as Understood

The authors present FDM-fabricated TPU/PLA tensegrity-inspired lattice structures as an impact-absorbing system for protecting payloads on future Mars landers. Bayesian optimization is employed to improve orientation-invariant energy absorption. Validation includes drop testing and "real-world field demonstrations."

## Strengths

**S1. Physical prototyping and testing is the right instinct.** The decision to build hardware and perform drop tests—including from multiple angles—reflects the kind of "build early, test often" mentality that accelerates technology maturation. This is encouraging for a student/early-career project.

**S2. Connecting structural innovation to a high-consequence application.** Using the Mars lander framing, while problematic (see weaknesses), does demonstrate the authors' ambition and awareness that passive energy-absorbing structures are relevant to planetary EDL. Tensegrity concepts for planetary landers have legitimate heritage in the literature (zhang2021optimizationforenergy pages 1-2, goyal2019analyticalstudyof pages 1-2, garanger2021softtensegritysystems pages 1-4).

**S3. Orientation-independence is a real design challenge for landers.** Landing orientation uncertainty is a genuine concern in EDL design. Mennu et al. (2024) show that pitch angle is a primary factor affecting peak acceleration in passive energy-absorbing landing systems (mennu2024analysisofa pages 1-13). Pursuing orientation-robust designs addresses a real engineering need.

## Weaknesses

**W1. PLA and TPU are not flight materials—this is a fundamental credibility problem.** PLA has a glass transition temperature of approximately 55–60°C and is biodegradable, hygroscopic, and prone to UV degradation. TPU, while more mechanically robust, is not qualified for vacuum, radiation, or thermal-cycling environments. For aerospace additive manufacturing in extreme environments, high-performance polymers such as PEEK, PEI (Ultem), and similar materials are required (aliberti2026additivemanufacturingof pages 6-7). Mars surface temperatures range from approximately −120°C to +20°C, with significant diurnal thermal cycling, UV flux unfiltered by a thick atmosphere, and near-vacuum pressures during transit. Neither PLA nor TPU has heritage or credible survivability in these conditions. The abstract makes no acknowledgment of this gap.

**W2. The Mars-lander framing overreaches the work's actual TRL.** This work is, at best, a TRL 1–2 terrestrial analog demonstrating a design methodology with surrogate materials. Framing it as contributing to "future Mars exploration techniques" and "future Mars landers" without acknowledging the enormous gap between FDM polymer prototypes and flight-qualified EDL hardware is misleading. For context, from the author's perspective at JPL, taking a concept from polymer prototype to flight-qualified metallic hardware for a mission involves materials qualification, environmental testing (ASTM E595 outgassing, thermal vacuum cycling, radiation exposure), structural analysis, and multi-year integration campaigns. The abstract should honestly position itself on the TRL ladder.

**W3. No comparison to heritage EDL energy-absorption systems.** Mars has seen multiple landing paradigms: Mars Pathfinder and MER used Vectran multi-layer airbags tested at impact velocities of ~60 ft/s (~18 m/s) on simulated rocky terrain (fasanella2009multiterrainearthlanding pages 3-6); Viking, Phoenix, and InSight used crushable aluminum honeycomb legs; and MSL/Perseverance used the Sky Crane hovering descent. Each of these is documented with specific mass fractions, peak deceleration limits, and energy-absorption capacities. The abstract neither cites nor compares against any of these heritage systems. Mennu et al. (2024) provide a contemporary example of how passive energy-absorbing composite structures for planetary payloads should be analyzed, including parametric studies of impact speed, pitch angle, and honeycomb sizing to achieve a 62% reduction in peak acceleration (mennu2024analysisofa pages 1-13).

**W4. No mission-relevant mass-efficiency metric.** A mission concept review would demand J/g (or J/kg) at a specified peak-deceleration constraint—not qualitative "successful payload protection." For tensegrity landers, Goyal et al. (2019) demonstrated that D-bar tensegrity systems achieve superior mass-to-energy-storage ratios compared to bent-buckled-beam alternatives (goyal2019analyticalstudyof pages 1-2). Zhang et al. (2021) noted that a tensegrity probe concept achieved a 50% payload mass fraction on Titan, more than twice that of conventional devices (zhang2021optimizationforenergy pages 1-2). These are the kinds of quantitative arguments a mission designer needs. The abstract provides none.

**W5. Environmental survivability is completely unaddressed.** Even setting aside PLA/TPU specifically, any material proposed for a Mars lander must address: (a) vacuum outgassing per ASTM E595 (total mass loss <1%, CVCM <0.1%), (b) thermal cycling over hundreds or thousands of cycles spanning the Martian temperature range, (c) UV and ionizing radiation exposure during transit and on the surface, and (d) long-duration storage (Mars transit is 7–9 months). FDM-printed polymers are known to exhibit interlayer delamination and void-induced crack initiation that worsens under environmental exposure (bustihan2026recentadvancesin pages 4-6, bustihan2026recentadvancesin pages 2-4). None of these concerns are mentioned.

**W6. "Real-world field demonstrations" is vague and potentially misleading.** What constitutes a "real-world field demonstration" for a Mars lander concept? Dropping a PLA/TPU prototype from a height on Earth does not validate Mars-relevant performance. Mars has 0.38 g surface gravity, ~6 mbar CO₂ atmosphere, and very different terrain properties than Earth surfaces. The phrase "high fidelity materials" is used without definition—high fidelity relative to what baseline?

**W7. No pathway from FDM polymer to flight-relevant materials and processes.** A credible abstract would sketch the material-transition roadmap: e.g., from FDM TPU/PLA proof-of-concept → SLM metallic lattice (Ti-6Al-4V, AlSi10Mg) → environmental qualification → integration with flight EDL architecture. Hofmann and colleagues at JPL have demonstrated this kind of technology infusion pathway for metallic glasses and compositionally graded metals, showing how AM prototypes translate to flight-qualified components through systematic material and process development (Hofmann et al., 2014; Oropeza et al., 2023). The abstract provides no such roadmap.

## Three Toughest Q&A Questions

**Q1.** "Have you evaluated whether PLA or TPU can survive the Mars transit environment—7+ months in vacuum with UV and radiation exposure—without catastrophic degradation, outgassing contamination of other spacecraft systems, or embrittlement at −120°C? What is your ASTM E595 data?"

**Q2.** "How does your structure's mass-specific energy absorption compare to the 13 kg/m² crushable aluminum honeycomb used on InSight's legs, or to the Vectran airbag system on MER that absorbed impacts at ~18 m/s? Can you provide a Ragone-style comparison (J/g vs. peak g-load) that would be meaningful to an EDL systems engineer?"

**Q3.** "If this is an early-stage methodology demonstrator—which is what the materials and test methods suggest—why is it framed as a Mars lander concept rather than as a Bayesian-optimization-driven design methodology for impact-absorbing cellular structures? Wouldn't reframing it as a generalizable design approach make the contribution clearer and more defensible?"

## Numerical Recommendation

**Score: 2 / 5 — Major Revision Required**

*Justification:* The Mars-lander framing undermines the abstract's credibility because the materials, processes, and testing conditions bear no relationship to the flight environment. However, if reframed as a terrestrial methodology demonstrator for Bayesian-optimized, orientation-robust impact absorbers—with a brief, honest acknowledgment that the approach could eventually be translated to flight-relevant materials—the work has value as an early-career innovation project. The current framing risks embarrassment at a symposium attended by practitioners who have actually put hardware on Mars.

---

# 3. SYNTHESIS

## Points of Agreement

Both reviewers converge on several critical assessments:

1. **The concept has early-stage merit** but is presented without the quantitative rigor expected even for a conference abstract. Both reviewers find the combination of tensegrity-inspired architecture, multi-angle testing, and Bayesian optimization to be a potentially interesting student-level contribution.

2. **The absence of quantitative metrics is the most damaging gap.** Neither reviewer can evaluate the claim of "successful payload protection" without SEA, peak transmitted force/acceleration, densification strain, or any other standard crashworthiness metric (shinde2022towardsanideal pages 1-2, shinde2022towardsanideal pages 4-5, mennu2024analysisofa pages 1-13).

3. **The lack of baseline comparisons renders the novelty claim unsupported.** Whether compared against established cellular-material topologies (Reviewer A's concern) or heritage EDL systems (Reviewer B's concern), the abstract fails to contextualize its contribution relative to the state of the art (shinde2022towardsanideal pages 1-2, zhang2021optimizationforenergy pages 1-2, fasanella2009multiterrainearthlanding pages 3-6).

4. **Both assign a score of 2/5 (Major Revision).** The work is not recommended for rejection outright because the concept and experimental initiative have value, but substantial revision is required before the abstract meets the standard for a TMS symposium on accelerating innovation.

## Conflicting Advice

1. **Framing:** Reviewer A would accept the Mars-lander framing if it were backed by rigorous energy-absorption mechanics and quantitative comparison to tensegrity and lattice baselines. Reviewer B fundamentally objects to the Mars-lander framing given the choice of PLA/TPU and the absence of any environmental survivability discussion. The resolution is likely Reviewer B's position: reframe as a terrestrial methodology demonstrator with a brief forward-looking statement about flight-material translation.

2. **Material focus:** Reviewer A sees PLA/TPU as acceptable for a proof-of-concept study of energy-absorption mechanics (following Bates et al. 2016 and Pajunen et al. 2019), provided the limitations are acknowledged. Reviewer B views PLA/TPU as disqualifying for any flight-relevant claim and would require at least a paragraph on the materials roadmap to metallic AM.

3. **Emphasis on testing rigor:** Reviewer A prioritizes strain-rate characterization and instrumented testing (accelerometers, force sensors, high-speed video per Pajunen et al. 2019 and Cronau & Engstler 2025). Reviewer B prioritizes environmental testing (outgassing, thermal cycling) and mission-relevant conditions (Mars gravity, terrain). Both are valid for their respective scopes.

## Prioritized List of Concrete Revisions

1. **Report quantitative metrics.** Include at minimum: SEA (J/g), peak transmitted acceleration (g), plateau stress (MPa), and densification strain (εD). Even preliminary values from the existing drop tests would transform the abstract.

2. **Reframe the application context honestly.** Replace "improve payload protection for future Mars landers" with language that positions this as a terrestrial analog or methodology demonstrator (TRL 1–2), with a forward-looking sentence about translation to flight-relevant materials.

3. **Add a baseline comparison.** Compare against at least one established architecture (e.g., FDM TPU hexagonal honeycomb at matched relative density) using the same test conditions. Bates et al. (2016) and Bustihan et al. (2025) provide readily available baselines (bustihan2025reusable3dprintedthermoplastic pages 1-2, bates20163dprintedpolyurethane pages 1-4).

4. **Specify the Bayesian optimization formulation.** State the objective function(s), design variable vector, constraint(s), surrogate model, acquisition function, and number of evaluations completed. The standards set by Mo et al. (2023) and Vangelatos et al. (2021) should guide this (mo2023accelerateddesignof pages 4-5, vangelatos2021strengththroughdefects pages 4-5).

5. **Clarify "tensegrity-like" vs. tensegrity.** Explain whether the structure has distinct tension and compression elements in self-stress (true tensegrity) or is a monolithic FDM print that mimics tensegrity geometry (tensegrity-inspired). Cite Pajunen et al. (2019) and Rimoli & Pal (2017) accordingly (pajunen2019designandimpact pages 7-8).

6. **Report test conditions and rate information.** Specify drop heights, impact velocities, strain rates, payload mass, and instrumentation. Acknowledge that polymers are strain-rate-sensitive and that quasi-static and dynamic behavior may differ substantially (cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 1-2, cronau2025energyabsorptionof pages 2-4).

7. **Acknowledge material limitations for space environments.** Even briefly, note that PLA/TPU serve as surrogate materials and that flight-relevant implementation would require environmental qualification and transition to aerospace-grade polymers or metals (aliberti2026additivemanufacturingof pages 6-7).

8. **Define "successful payload protection."** Replace this qualitative phrase with a quantitative success criterion (e.g., "peak payload acceleration below 100 g" or "no structural failure at impact energies up to X J").

## Consolidated Key Reference List

The following table compiles the references both reviewers would expect the authors to know and cite:

| Reference | Relevance Category | Why Critical |
|---|---|---|
| Shinde et al., 2022, *Towards an Ideal Energy Absorber* | Energy Absorption Metrics/Baselines | Defines and compares the key crashworthiness metrics the abstract currently omits—SEA, maximum transmitted stress, plateau behavior, and densification efficiency—across honeycomb, lattice, and TPMS baselines; essential for Reviewer A’s demand for quantitative benchmarking (shinde2022towardsanideal pages 1-2, shinde2022towardsanideal pages 4-5, shinde2022towardsanideal pages 2-4) |
| Tuninetti et al., 2025, *Biomimetic Lattice Structures* | Energy Absorption Metrics/Baselines | Summarizes how hierarchical and bio-inspired lattices improve SEA, crushing force efficiency, and plateau stress relative to conventional architectures; useful for arguing why a new unit cell is mechanistically justified (tuninetti2025biomimeticlatticestructures pages 12-14) |

*Table: This table summarizes how the two mock reviewers would likely assess the abstract from different technical vantage points. It highlights shared enthusiasm for the concept but converges on a major-revision recommendation for different reasons: mechanics rigor for Reviewer A and flight-credibility/TRL realism for Reviewer B.*

---

# 1. REVIEW A — Reviewer A (Cordero-Style Persona: Architected Materials and Energy-Absorption Mechanics)

## Summary of Contribution as Understood

The authors propose a non-prismatic, hexagon-based, tensegrity-inspired lattice configuration fabricated via FDM from TPU and PLA. The stated goal is to protect a payload under high-impact conditions, with the motivating application being future Mars landers. Bayesian optimization is employed to tune the unit-cell geometry for orientation-insensitive impact absorption. Validation is pursued through controlled drop testing and field demonstrations across multiple impact angles.

## Strengths

**S1. Timely combination of tensegrity-inspired architecture with optimization.** The tensegrity-inspired lattice concept for impact absorption is grounded in a growing literature. Tensegrity structures are inherently free-standing, packable, and capable of absorbing large impact loads while maintaining load-bearing capability even after severe deformation (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000010). Combining this with Bayesian optimization for geometry is a contemporary and well-motivated approach.

**S2. Experimental orientation is commendable.** The decision to physically build and drop-test prototypes, rather than relying solely on simulation, is valuable. Drop testing of tensegrity-inspired structures has been shown to reveal important phenomena—such as material hysteresis-dominated energy dissipation and load-limiting behavior—that cannot be captured by quasi-static analysis alone (pqac-00000011, pqac-00000028).

**S3. Multi-angle testing to address anisotropy is well-motivated.** Orientation-dependent energy absorption is a recognized challenge in lattice structures, where functionally graded and hybrid gradient designs have been developed specifically to enhance directional robustness (pqac-00000030). Acknowledging and testing for this is appropriate.

**S4. Use of Bayesian optimization for a physically expensive design loop.** Bayesian optimization is well-suited to problems where each evaluation is costly (here, physical drop tests). The literature demonstrates that BO can converge with as few as 15–250 high-fidelity evaluations for architected-material problems with 16–17 design variables (pqac-00000016, pqac-00000021).

## Weaknesses

**W1. Complete absence of quantitative energy-absorption metrics.** The abstract reports no specific energy absorption (SEA), plateau stress, densification strain, stroke efficiency, crush force efficiency, or peak transmitted force values. In the established energy-absorption literature, an ideal absorber is assessed on at least four criteria: (a) the relationship between SEA and maximum transmitted stress, (b) plateau stress undulation, (c) densification efficiency, and (d) design tunability (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001). Without any of these, the claim of "successful payload protection" is unverifiable. Even qualitative trends (e.g., SEA vs. relative density) would substantially strengthen the abstract.

**W2. No baseline comparison against established architectures.** The energy-absorption field has well-characterized baselines. For example, TPMS structures (diamond, gyroid) have been shown to outperform honeycomb and beam-lattice structures in SEA-to-maximum-stress ratios and densification efficiencies, while honeycomb structures occupy an intermediate position (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000007). TPU honeycombs fabricated by FDM achieve energy absorption up to 0.34 J/cm³ (pqac-00000037), and bio-inspired curved-elliptical lattices achieve SEA of 24.6 J/g with crush force efficiency exceeding octet and BCC lattices by 15–35% (pqac-00000003). Without benchmarking against any of these, the hexagon-based tensegrity cell's value proposition cannot be assessed.

**W3. Mechanistic rationale for the hexagon-based tensegrity unit cell is missing.** Why hexagonal? Why tensegrity-inspired rather than a true tensegrity (D-bar, truncated octahedron), which has analytical support for mass-efficient energy absorption that can exceed bent-buckled-beam approaches (pqac-00000009)? The term "tensegrity-like" is imprecise—the distinction between a true tensegrity (separate tension/compression elements in self-stress) and a monolithic FDM lattice that merely mimics the geometry is mechanistically important. Pajunen et al. (2019) carefully distinguish "tensegrity-inspired" structures fabricated as monolithic prints, acknowledging that these exhibit materially different energy-dissipation mechanisms (material hysteresis vs. elastic energy storage) from classical tensegrity (pqac-00000011).

**W4. Quasi-static vs. dynamic testing validity is unaddressed.** Polymers exhibit strain-rate-dependent mechanical properties, making strain rate testing critical for obtaining applicable data for impact scenarios (pqac-00000025). Cronau & Engstler (2025) demonstrate that quasi-static tests cannot represent material behavior under high strain rates and use drop-tower testing at 5 m/s to generate strain rates of ~150 s⁻¹ (pqac-00000027). The abstract mentions "controlled drop testing" and "field demonstrations" but provides no information on impact velocities, strain rates, or how these relate to the target application's loading regime.

**W5. Bayesian optimization loop is under-specified.** A well-posed BO for energy-absorbing architected materials requires: (a) clearly defined objective function(s) (e.g., maximize SEA subject to peak-force constraints), (b) enumerated design variables (e.g., strut widths, angles, relative density), (c) a strategy for handling experimental noise (drop-test variability), and (d) a surrogate model choice. In Mo et al. (2023), the BO explicitly optimizes energy absorption with constraints on plateau stress variation and relative density using a multifidelity Gaussian process, converging in ~15 high-fidelity experiments (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000021). Vangelatos et al. (2021) optimize 17 design variables with careful noise handling (7% SD) and an acquisition function strategy (pqac-00000023). The abstract provides none of these details—stating only "Bayesian optimization of lattice base-unit geometry" without specifying objectives, variables, or noise treatment.

**W6. FDM process-parameter and material variability are ignored.** FDM-printed parts exhibit inherent anisotropy, interlayer delamination, and void-induced crack initiation that can prematurely truncate energy absorption (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035). Bates et al. (2016) show that TPU energy absorption is significantly dependent on both strain rate and cell orientation (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037). The abstract does not acknowledge or control for these well-documented sources of variability.

**W7. "Successful payload protection" is not a scientific metric.** The claim of "successful payload protection across a range of testing conditions" is qualitative and unfalsifiable without defining success criteria (e.g., peak transmitted acceleration below X g, energy absorbed per unit mass above Y J/g). Mennu et al. (2024) demonstrate that even for passive energy-absorbing landing systems, peak acceleration is the critical metric, with pitch angle and impact speed identified as primary factors (pqac-00000013, pqac-00000014).

## Three Toughest Q&A Questions

**Q1.** "You claim 'successful payload protection'—can you provide the specific energy absorption (J/g), the peak transmitted force or acceleration (g), and the densification strain of your structure? How do these compare to a simple FDM-printed TPU hexagonal honeycomb of the same relative density, which Bates et al. (2016) characterized at 0.01–0.34 J/cm³?"

**Q2.** "Your Bayesian optimization has an objective—what is it, exactly? Is it minimizing peak transmitted force, maximizing SEA, minimizing the coefficient of variation of absorbed energy across orientations, or some multi-objective combination? How many evaluations has your BO loop completed, and how do you handle the stochastic noise inherent in drop-test measurements?"

**Q3.** "What is the mechanistic energy-absorption mode of your structure—is it elastic buckling and recovery (as in Pajunen et al.'s tensegrity-inspired prints), plastic hinge formation, material hysteresis, or some combination? Does your structure survive multiple impacts, and does it exhibit the load-limiting plateau behavior that makes tensegrity structures attractive for impact mitigation?"

## Numerical Recommendation

**Score: 2 / 5 — Major Revision Required**

*Justification:* The concept has merit as an early-stage exploration, but the abstract falls well below the quantitative and mechanistic rigor expected for an energy-absorption contribution. The absence of any crashworthiness metrics, baseline comparisons, or specification of the BO formulation means the abstract cannot currently demonstrate a contribution beyond what is already established in the tensegrity-for-impact and FDM-lattice-energy-absorption literatures. The work would be strengthened substantially by: reporting at least SEA, peak force, and densification strain; comparing against a simple honeycomb or foam baseline at matched relative density; and specifying the BO objective, design variables, and noise model.

---

# 2. REVIEW B — Reviewer B (Hofmann-Style Persona: Spacecraft Materials, EDL Heritage, Technology Infusion)

## Summary of Contribution as Understood

The authors present FDM-fabricated TPU/PLA tensegrity-inspired lattice structures as an impact-absorbing system for protecting payloads on future Mars landers. Bayesian optimization is employed to improve orientation-invariant energy absorption. Validation includes drop testing and "real-world field demonstrations."

## Strengths

**S1. Physical prototyping and testing is the right instinct.** The decision to build hardware and perform drop tests—including from multiple angles—reflects the kind of "build early, test often" mentality that accelerates technology maturation. This is encouraging for a student/early-career project.

**S2. Connecting structural innovation to a high-consequence application.** Using the Mars lander framing, while problematic (see weaknesses), does demonstrate the authors' ambition and awareness that passive energy-absorbing structures are relevant to planetary EDL. Tensegrity concepts for planetary landers have legitimate heritage in the literature (pqac-00000008, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010).

**S3. Orientation-independence is a real design challenge for landers.** Landing orientation uncertainty is a genuine concern in EDL design. Mennu et al. (2024) show that pitch angle is a primary factor affecting peak acceleration in passive energy-absorbing landing systems (pqac-00000013). Pursuing orientation-robust designs addresses a real engineering need.

## Weaknesses

**W1. PLA and TPU are not flight materials—this is a fundamental credibility problem.** PLA has a glass transition temperature of approximately 55–60°C and is biodegradable, hygroscopic, and prone to UV degradation. TPU, while more mechanically robust, is not qualified for vacuum, radiation, or thermal-cycling environments. For aerospace additive manufacturing in extreme environments, high-performance polymers such as PEEK, PEI (Ultem), and similar materials are required (pqac-00000024). Mars surface temperatures range from approximately −120°C to +20°C, with significant diurnal thermal cycling, UV flux unfiltered by a thick atmosphere, and near-vacuum pressures during transit. Neither PLA nor TPU has heritage or credible survivability in these conditions. The abstract makes no acknowledgment of this gap.

**W2. The Mars-lander framing overreaches the work's actual TRL.** This work is, at best, a TRL 1–2 terrestrial analog demonstrating a design methodology with surrogate materials. Framing it as contributing to "future Mars exploration techniques" and "future Mars landers" without acknowledging the enormous gap between FDM polymer prototypes and flight-qualified EDL hardware is misleading. For context, from the author's perspective at JPL, taking a concept from polymer prototype to flight-qualified metallic hardware for a mission involves materials qualification, environmental testing (ASTM E595 outgassing, thermal vacuum cycling, radiation exposure), structural analysis, and multi-year integration campaigns. The abstract should honestly position itself on the TRL ladder.

**W3. No comparison to heritage EDL energy-absorption systems.** Mars has seen multiple landing paradigms: Mars Pathfinder and MER used Vectran multi-layer airbags tested at impact velocities of ~60 ft/s (~18 m/s) on simulated rocky terrain (pqac-00000012); Viking, Phoenix, and InSight used crushable aluminum honeycomb legs; and MSL/Perseverance used the Sky Crane hovering descent. Each of these is documented with specific mass fractions, peak deceleration limits, and energy-absorption capacities. The abstract neither cites nor compares against any of these heritage systems. Mennu et al. (2024) provide a contemporary example of how passive energy-absorbing composite structures for planetary payloads should be analyzed, including parametric studies of impact speed, pitch angle, and honeycomb sizing to achieve a 62% reduction in peak acceleration (pqac-00000013).

**W4. No mission-relevant mass-efficiency metric.** A mission concept review would demand J/g (or J/kg) at a specified peak-deceleration constraint—not qualitative "successful payload protection." For tensegrity landers, Goyal et al. (2019) demonstrated that D-bar tensegrity systems achieve superior mass-to-energy-storage ratios compared to bent-buckled-beam alternatives (pqac-00000009). Zhang et al. (2021) noted that a tensegrity probe concept achieved a 50% payload mass fraction on Titan, more than twice that of conventional devices (pqac-00000008). These are the kinds of quantitative arguments a mission designer needs. The abstract provides none.

**W5. Environmental survivability is completely unaddressed.** Even setting aside PLA/TPU specifically, any material proposed for a Mars lander must address: (a) vacuum outgassing per ASTM E595 (total mass loss <1%, CVCM <0.1%), (b) thermal cycling over hundreds or thousands of cycles spanning the Martian temperature range, (c) UV and ionizing radiation exposure during transit and on the surface, and (d) long-duration storage (Mars transit is 7–9 months). FDM-printed polymers are known to exhibit interlayer delamination and void-induced crack initiation that worsens under environmental exposure (pqac-00000033, pqac-00000035). None of these concerns are mentioned.

**W6. "Real-world field demonstrations" is vague and potentially misleading.** What constitutes a "real-world field demonstration" for a Mars lander concept? Dropping a PLA/TPU prototype from a height on Earth does not validate Mars-relevant performance. Mars has 0.38 g surface gravity, ~6 mbar CO₂ atmosphere, and very different terrain properties than Earth surfaces. The phrase "high fidelity materials" is used without definition—high fidelity relative to what baseline?

**W7. No pathway from FDM polymer to flight-relevant materials and processes.** A credible abstract would sketch the material-transition roadmap: e.g., from FDM TPU/PLA proof-of-concept → SLM metallic lattice (Ti-6Al-4V, AlSi10Mg) → environmental qualification → integration with flight EDL architecture. Hofmann and colleagues at JPL have demonstrated this kind of technology infusion pathway for metallic glasses and compositionally graded metals, showing how AM prototypes translate to flight-qualified components through systematic material and process development (Hofmann et al., 2014; Oropeza et al., 2023). The abstract provides no such roadmap.

## Three Toughest Q&A Questions

**Q1.** "Have you evaluated whether PLA or TPU can survive the Mars transit environment—7+ months in vacuum with UV and radiation exposure—without catastrophic degradation, outgassing contamination of other spacecraft systems, or embrittlement at −120°C? What is your ASTM E595 data?"

**Q2.** "How does your structure's mass-specific energy absorption compare to the 13 kg/m² crushable aluminum honeycomb used on InSight's legs, or to the Vectran airbag system on MER that absorbed impacts at ~18 m/s? Can you provide a Ragone-style comparison (J/g vs. peak g-load) that would be meaningful to an EDL systems engineer?"

**Q3.** "If this is an early-stage methodology demonstrator—which is what the materials and test methods suggest—why is it framed as a Mars lander concept rather than as a Bayesian-optimization-driven design methodology for impact-absorbing cellular structures? Wouldn't reframing it as a generalizable design approach make the contribution clearer and more defensible?"

## Numerical Recommendation

**Score: 2 / 5 — Major Revision Required**

*Justification:* The Mars-lander framing undermines the abstract's credibility because the materials, processes, and testing conditions bear no relationship to the flight environment. However, if reframed as a terrestrial methodology demonstrator for Bayesian-optimized, orientation-robust impact absorbers—with a brief, honest acknowledgment that the approach could eventually be translated to flight-relevant materials—the work has value as an early-career innovation project. The current framing risks embarrassment at a symposium attended by practitioners who have actually put hardware on Mars.

---

# 3. SYNTHESIS

## Points of Agreement

Both reviewers converge on several critical assessments:

1. **The concept has early-stage merit** but is presented without the quantitative rigor expected even for a conference abstract. Both reviewers find the combination of tensegrity-inspired architecture, multi-angle testing, and Bayesian optimization to be a potentially interesting student-level contribution.

2. **The absence of quantitative metrics is the most damaging gap.** Neither reviewer can evaluate the claim of "successful payload protection" without SEA, peak transmitted force/acceleration, densification strain, or any other standard crashworthiness metric (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000013).

3. **The lack of baseline comparisons renders the novelty claim unsupported.** Whether compared against established cellular-material topologies (Reviewer A's concern) or heritage EDL systems (Reviewer B's concern), the abstract fails to contextualize its contribution relative to the state of the art (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000008, pqac-00000012).

4. **Both assign a score of 2/5 (Major Revision).** The work is not recommended for rejection outright because the concept and experimental initiative have value, but substantial revision is required before the abstract meets the standard for a TMS symposium on accelerating innovation.

## Conflicting Advice

1. **Framing:** Reviewer A would accept the Mars-lander framing if it were backed by rigorous energy-absorption mechanics and quantitative comparison to tensegrity and lattice baselines. Reviewer B fundamentally objects to the Mars-lander framing given the choice of PLA/TPU and the absence of any environmental survivability discussion. The resolution is likely Reviewer B's position: reframe as a terrestrial methodology demonstrator with a brief forward-looking statement about flight-material translation.

2. **Material focus:** Reviewer A sees PLA/TPU as acceptable for a proof-of-concept study of energy-absorption mechanics (following Bates et al. 2016 and Pajunen et al. 2019), provided the limitations are acknowledged. Reviewer B views PLA/TPU as disqualifying for any flight-relevant claim and would require at least a paragraph on the materials roadmap to metallic AM.

3. **Emphasis on testing rigor:** Reviewer A prioritizes strain-rate characterization and instrumented testing (accelerometers, force sensors, high-speed video per Pajunen et al. 2019 and Cronau & Engstler 2025). Reviewer B prioritizes environmental testing (outgassing, thermal cycling) and mission-relevant conditions (Mars gravity, terrain). Both are valid for their respective scopes.

## Prioritized List of Concrete Revisions

1. **Report quantitative metrics.** Include at minimum: SEA (J/g), peak transmitted acceleration (g), plateau stress (MPa), and densification strain (εD). Even preliminary values from the existing drop tests would transform the abstract.

2. **Reframe the application context honestly.** Replace "improve payload protection for future Mars landers" with language that positions this as a terrestrial analog or methodology demonstrator (TRL 1–2), with a forward-looking sentence about translation to flight-relevant materials.

3. **Add a baseline comparison.** Compare against at least one established architecture (e.g., FDM TPU hexagonal honeycomb at matched relative density) using the same test conditions. Bates et al. (2016) and Bustihan et al. (2025) provide readily available baselines (pqac-00000032, pqac-00000037).

4. **Specify the Bayesian optimization formulation.** State the objective function(s), design variable vector, constraint(s), surrogate model, acquisition function, and number of evaluations completed. The standards set by Mo et al. (2023) and Vangelatos et al. (2021) should guide this (pqac-00000020, pqac-00000023).

5. **Clarify "tensegrity-like" vs. tensegrity.** Explain whether the structure has distinct tension and compression elements in self-stress (true tensegrity) or is a monolithic FDM print that mimics tensegrity geometry (tensegrity-inspired). Cite Pajunen et al. (2019) and Rimoli & Pal (2017) accordingly (pqac-00000011).

6. **Report test conditions and rate information.** Specify drop heights, impact velocities, strain rates, payload mass, and instrumentation. Acknowledge that polymers are strain-rate-sensitive and that quasi-static and dynamic behavior may differ substantially (pqac-00000025, pqac-00000027).

7. **Acknowledge material limitations for space environments.** Even briefly, note that PLA/TPU serve as surrogate materials and that flight-relevant implementation would require environmental qualification and transition to aerospace-grade polymers or metals (pqac-00000024).

8. **Define "successful payload protection."** Replace this qualitative phrase with a quantitative success criterion (e.g., "peak payload acceleration below 100 g" or "no structural failure at impact energies up to X J").

| Tuninetti et al., 2025, *Biomimetic Lattice Structures* | Energy Absorption Metrics/Baselines | Summarizes how hierarchical and bio-inspired lattices improve SEA, crushing force efficiency, and plateau stress relative to conventional architectures; useful for arguing why a new unit cell is mechanistically justified (pqac-00000003) |

| Bates et al., 2016, *3D Printed Polyurethane Honeycombs* | FDM Polymer Energy Absorption | A foundational FFF/TPU energy-absorption paper showing orientation and strain-rate sensitivity, elastic recovery, and comparison to polyurethane foams; directly relevant to the abstract’s TPU/FDM prototype claims (pqac-00000036, pqac-00000037) |

---

This dual-review analysis indicates that while the abstract describes a promising early-stage research direction combining tensegrity-inspired architectures, FDM prototyping, and Bayesian optimization, it currently lacks the quantitative mechanics data, baseline comparisons, and honest TRL positioning needed to be competitive at TMS Symposium 105. Addressing the prioritized revisions above—particularly reporting crashworthiness metrics and reframing the application context—would substantially strengthen the submission for a venue focused on accelerating materials innovation.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses key metrics for evaluating energy absorption in additively manufactured cellular structures under compression. Primary metrics include: (1) first maximum/peak stress—the highest stress before initial drop; (2) plateau stress—average stress in the region between first peak and densification onset; (3) plateau slope—indicating hardening or softening behavior, with flatter plateaus preferred for energy absorption; (4) plateau undulation (ULC)—measuring waviness indicative of localized failure patterns, with ideal absorbers having ULC values near 0; and (5) densification strain onset—critical for computing energy absorption. The excerpt focuses on beam-based lattices (BCC) and triply periodic minimal surfaces (TPMS), with P-type TPMS geometry showing plateau slopes less dependent on relative density. Energy absorption behavior is primarily influenced by base material properties, relative density, and cell geometry. Specific values for various materials and geometries are presented in a comparative table, though detailed topological comparisons are limited in this section.

contexts.context: This research studied six cellular structures (hexagonal honeycomb, auxetic and Voronoi lattice, and diamond, gyroid, and Schwarz-P TPMS) under quasistatic compression to compare energy absorption performance. The study assessed four key criteria: the relationship between specific energy absorption (SEA) and maximum transmitted stress, stress plateau undulation, densification efficiency, and design tunability. Results showed that TPMS structures, particularly diamond and gyroid, had the best overall performance with superior SEA and lower maximum transmitted stresses. Honeycomb structures performed intermediately between TPMS and lattice types. Auxetic and Voronoi lattice structures had low SEA relative to maximum transmitted stresses and low densification efficiencies, though they were highly tunable. The research highlights that energy absorption optimization involves multiple interdependent metrics including peak load, plateau slope uniformity, energy absorption efficiency, densification strain, and specific energy absorption, and that structures may excel in one metric while performing poorly in others.

contexts.context: The excerpt discusses specific energy absorption (SEA) metrics for lattice structures, defined as energy absorbed per unit mass and calculated using the Gibson–Ashby framework formula: SEA = (σ∗/ρ∗) = (σs/ρs)·(ρ∗/ρs)0.5. Key findings indicate that higher-density lattices absorb more energy, which is important for crashworthiness and impact protection applications. The study compares different lattice topologies, showing that stretch-dominated lattices (octet-truss, BCC) significantly outperform bending-dominated structures (honeycombs, pyramidal) in terms of strength and stiffness because they distribute loads more efficiently. Specifically, the octet-truss lattice with 0.23 relative density achieved 0.056 energy absorption and 0.110 relative strength, while equal-strength BCC lattices showed 0.076 relative strength, exceeding traditional honeycomb values of 0.058–0.070. The excerpt does not provide information on plateau stress, densification strain, stroke efficiency, crush force efficiency, TPMS, foam, or tensegrity structures.

contexts.context: This paper discusses key energy absorption metrics for cellular structures. Specific Energy Absorption (SEA) is a mass-normalized measure calculated from the area under the stress-strain curve up to densification strain (εD). The densification strain is vital for energy absorption computation and can be defined using four different approaches: energy efficiency method, predefined strain values (typically 40-50%), first maximum stress threshold, or intersection of plateau and densification region slopes. Energy absorption efficiency (η) compares a material's energy absorption to an ideal absorber for a given maximum stress. An ideal energy absorber has: (a) predictable peak stress-relative density relationship, (b) flat plateau maintaining stress below peak, and (c) ability to absorb needed energy before densification. The study compares three categories of cellular materials: honeycombs, beam-based lattices, and TPMS structures (diamond, gyroid, Schwarz-P). The paper notes that plateau stress, energy absorbed per unit volume, and peak stress are commonly reported metrics, though it focuses on deeper correlation between cellular geometry and energy absorption metrics.

contexts.context: Tensegrity structures are self-standing, lightweight structures consisting of bars in compression and cables in tension that have emerged as promising energy absorbers for aerospace applications, particularly planetary landers. Their key advantages include being free-standing without requiring supports, packable into compact sizes for launch, and capable of absorbing large impact loads while protecting interior systems. Research demonstrates superior performance compared to conventional systems: a tensegrity probe concept achieved a 50% payload mass fraction on Titan, more than twice that of conventional devices. The D-bar tensegrity system showed efficient energy absorption compared to buckled bent beams. Tensegrity lattices achieve superior strength in low-density regimes due to nonlinear geometric effects and buckling of compression members. The structures demonstrate excellent impact tolerance because their load-bearing capability remains intact even after severe deformation. This paper specifically addresses optimization of 3D tensegrity lattices with truncated octahedral units to maximize energy absorption through controlled buckling and prestress design.

contexts.context: This article investigates D-bar tensegrity systems as lightweight mechanical energy absorption components for aerospace applications like planetary landers. The research derives analytical equations for elastic energy storage in D-bar systems of varying complexity for the first time. The study compares D-bar systems with bent buckled beams used in flexible-bar tensegrity concepts. Results demonstrate that D-bar systems of low complexity outperform bent buckled beams by storing more energy while requiring less mass at both the component level and when integrated into planetary lander assemblies. The approach stores energy in strings and bars without triggering local structural instabilities like buckling, enabling more reliable structures. contexts.context: This paper presents a Bayesian optimization approach (EMCS framework) for designing optimal microlattice structures. The design space includes 17 variables: 16 qualitative variables representing unit cell types (four states: unblemished or defected with varying missing members) arranged in a 4×4×5 array, and 1 binary orientation variable (face or edge connection). The primary objective is maximizing strain energy density while maintaining structural integrity. The authors use critical buckling load (Pc) as a proxy cost function rather than direct strain energy density calculation, reducing computational cost by formulating it as an eigenvalue problem in the elastic domain. This approach is more sample-efficient than other optimization algorithms for mixed variable problems. The method demonstrates robustness to fabrication variations in elastic modulus and Poisson's ratio, achieving four orders of magnitude improvement over existing microlattice structures in normalized strain energy density.

contexts.context: This work applies multifidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) to design nonuniform 2D cellular lattice structures. The design space consists of 16 parameters representing strut widths in triangular elements, bounded between 0.5-1 mm. Three objectives are optimized: energy absorption (Eab), plateau stress variation (var(σpl)), and relative density. Energy absorption is computed as the area under the stress-strain curve bounded by the densification slope. Bayesian optimization offers advantages including requiring minimal initial data points, inherent uncertainty quantification through Gaussian processes, and ease of implementation. The framework combines low-fidelity numerical simulations with high-fidelity experiments in parallel, addressing limitations of simulation-only or experiment-only optimization approaches. This multifidelity approach allows efficient exploration of the design space while incorporating real experimental data to validate numerical predictions.

contexts.context: This paper presents a Bayesian optimization (BO) framework called EMCS for optimizing architected microlattice materials. The design variables consist of 17 inputs representing unit cells in a 4×4 array and their orientations, treated as mixed qualitative and quantitative variables. The primary objective is to maximize strain energy density while maintaining structural integrity. The optimization uses critical buckling load (Pc) as a proxy for energy absorption, as minimizing Pc leads to exponential increases in strain energy density at fracture. The method achieves sample efficiency by finding the global minimum for a 17-dimensional problem (8.58×10^9 combinations) within 250 function evaluations. The EMCS framework uses Bayes' theorem to leverage information from previous evaluations, employing an exploration-exploitation strategy to avoid local minima. A surrogate model guides the search through acquisition functions (SMC in this case), enabling efficient optimization despite expensive finite element analysis (FEA) computations required for cost function evaluation.

snippets: We use a previously unexplored Bayesian optimization framework, "evolutionary Monte Carlo sampling," to systematically design the arrangement of defects in an architected microlattice to maximize its strain energy density before undergoing catastrophic failure.
Each site of the microlattice can choose between four different unit cells and can have two different orientations of attachment, yielding a large combinatorial design space.
Our algorithm searches a design space with billions of 4 × 4 × 5 3D lattices, yet it finds the global optimum with only 250 cost function evaluations.
Bayesian optimization (BO) has proven to work well for optimization problems with costly black-box functions by finding global optimum with minimum number of function calls
We introduce a novel BO framework, which we term "evolutionary Monte Carlo sampling" (EMCS), to optimize the prohibitively expensive qualitative input design space
we introduce "stochastic Monte Carlo" (SMC) acquisition function as part of the EMCS framework, which outperforms the existing acquisition functions used in literature for qualitative variables

contexts.context: This excerpt describes a Bayesian optimization (BO) framework for optimizing architected materials using Gaussian Processes (GP) as surrogate models. The approach uses Bayes' theorem to update posterior distributions based on data, achieving global optima with only 250 function evaluations including 50 initial random inputs. The method employs an acquisition function 𝒜(x) that balances exploration and exploitation. For mixed discrete-qualitative variable spaces, genetic algorithms (GA) are used to minimize the acquisition function since standard gradient methods are ineffective. The surrogate model uses a capped distance kernel with hyperparameters controlling the GP shape. Leave-one-out cross-validation optimizes hyperparameter fitting. While the excerpt focuses on optimization methodology and benchmarking on test functions rather than specific energy absorption objectives, it demonstrates the sample efficiency and computational efficiency of the BO approach for expensive black-box function evaluations like finite element analysis (FEA).

contexts.context: This paper applies multifidelity Bayesian optimization (MFBO) to design triangular lattice structures for maximal energy absorption during compression. The design space includes 16 independent continuous variables defining the lattice geometry. The method combines high-fidelity experimental data (physical compression tests) with low-fidelity simulation data (ABAQUS finite element analysis) to improve sample efficiency. A key advantage is convergence with only 15 high-fidelity experiments, compared to single-fidelity approaches requiring 250+ iterations. The paper incorporates constraints on plateau stress variance in the acquisition function. The multifidelity approach leverages correlation between experiments and simulations to allow parallel low-fidelity data collection, accelerating convergence. The surrogate model uses Bayesian optimization to predict energy absorption and guide the search toward optimal lattice designs while balancing exploration with constraint satisfaction.

contexts.context: This paper presents a multifidelity Bayesian optimization framework for designing architected materials optimized for energy absorption during compression. The approach combines high-fidelity physical experiments with low-fidelity numerical simulations fed in parallel to train a Gaussian process surrogate model. The framework iteratively selects which experiments and simulations to conduct next to find optimal structural parameters. Key advantages include improved sample efficiency—requiring fewer iterations to find the optimum compared to single high-fidelity approaches, reducing material costs and time. The method incorporates constraints on relative density and stress variations. Design constraints and objectives can be applied to find optimal structures within specified bounds. The Bayesian optimization approach requires minimal initial data, inherently handles uncertainty through the Gaussian process, and offers ease of implementation—making it practical for complex, labor-intensive experiments while automating low-fidelity simulations.

The primary objective is maximizing energy absorption (Eab) with constraints on stress variation and relative density. The surrogate model employs a multifidelity Gaussian process incorporating both high-fidelity experiments and low-fidelity numerical simulations. Regarding noise handling, the approach leverages the strong linear correlation between high and low-fidelity data streams, with both sources integrated simultaneously in the surrogate model. The optimization reveals different deformation patterns: layer-by-layer crushing for maximum energy absorption objectives, versus V-shaped buckling when minimizing stress variation.

contexts.context: This article presents a Bayesian optimization (BO) framework for optimizing architected microlattice structures. The design problem involves 17 categorical variables with four possible values each. The key innovation is the EMCS (Efficient Mixed variable Categorical Space) framework that adapts BO to discrete, qualitative inputs using a constrained genetic algorithm (GA), rather than traditional continuous optimization methods. The study introduces the SMC acquisition function that outperforms existing methods for categorical variables in anisotropic parameter spaces. Sample efficiency is notably high—only 250 evaluations were needed compared to orders of magnitude more for genetic algorithms. Noise handling incorporates 0.005 noise variance (7% SD) to account for fabrication imperfections and experimental measurement uncertainty. The objective focuses on optimizing buckling load and energy absorption through microscopic instability patterns that enable densification while preventing catastrophic fracture. The optimized finite lattice array can serve as a building block for creating large structures with high energy absorption capacity.

contexts.context: This excerpt describes a comprehensive drop testing methodology for 3D-printed tensegrity-inspired structures. The experimental setup includes a low-friction vertical rod with a free-falling striker mass (100g or 200g steel), an accelerometer to record impact acceleration, a triaxial ceramic shear accelerometer with 0.47 mV/(m/s²) sensitivity, and a quartz force sensor measuring reaction forces. A high-speed camera (1000 fps) captures displacement data with tracked markers. The structure sits on a glass sheet with acetone to reduce friction. Dynamic ABAQUS simulations were developed to compare with drop test experiments, exploring various impact velocities. The methodology addresses impact velocity control through striker height variation and synchronized time measurement between camera and oscilloscope data. contexts.context: This paper describes FFF 3D printing of thermoplastic polyurethanes (TPUs) for creating tailorable, flexible cellular structures designed for energy absorption. The study demonstrates that TPUs are excellent candidates for energy-absorbing applications due to their superior impact properties and abrasion resistance compared to other 3D-printable flexible materials. The research presents a parametric study of hexagonal honeycomb arrays manufactured from TPUs with relative densities of 0.18-0.49, tested at strain rates of 0.03-0.3s⁻¹. The structures achieved energy absorption capabilities of 0.01-0.34 J/cm³ with elastic recovery, reaching maximum energy absorbing efficiency of 0.36, comparable to traditional expanded closed-cell polyurethane foams. The paper emphasizes that energy absorption behavior is significantly dependent on strain rate and cell orientation. FFF offers advantages over selective laser sintering (SLS) in producing lower porosity parts and allowing closed-cell structures.
